Dictionary

Concepts, infrastructure, and ideas from the pre-web internet era — explained for people who weren't there.

Online vs. Internet
Entry 001  ·  Infrastructure  ·  Networking  ·  Pre-Web Era

Online But Not Internet

How CompuServe, AOL, and Prodigy were connected services without being the internet — and how they physically worked

+
The core distinction

The Internet is an open protocol — a shared agreement that any computer, anywhere, can speak. Nobody owns it. An online service is a private network owned by one company, accessible only through their infrastructure. Same copper wires underneath. Completely different philosophy on top.

What "online" meant before the internet existed

In 1985, if someone said they were "online," they meant they had dialed into a private commercial network — CompuServe, The Source, or a few others — using a modem connected to their telephone. There was no World Wide Web. There was no public internet to speak of. "Online" specifically meant "connected to one of these services."

These services were not connected to each other. If you had a CompuServe account and your friend had a Prodigy account, you could not email each other. You were on separate networks with no bridge between them — like two telephone systems in different countries with no international calling. Your email address only worked inside CompuServe. CompuServe's forums only existed inside CompuServe. The whole universe of what was possible was bounded by what one company decided to build.

This is called a walled garden. Everything is curated, controlled, and owned by one entity. You get in through their door, see what they decide to show you, and leave the same way you came in.

How the physical network worked

Every keystroke you typed on your home computer traveled through three distinct physical layers before reaching the mainframe in Columbus, Ohio — and came back the same way. The diagram below shows CompuServe's actual network architecture. Every line represents real copper wire in the ground.

CompuServe Information Service physical network architecture, c. 1985 — 1989

Layer by layer

Your home computer did no computing. It was a display terminal — showing whatever Columbus sent down the wire and forwarding your keystrokes back up. A faster home computer gave you no advantage. The intelligence was entirely at the other end.

The modem converted digital data into sound. Your telephone network was designed for human voice — it could only carry frequencies in the range of normal speech. A modem (modulator-demodulator) converted your data into audio tones that could travel over those voice lines, then converted them back at the other end. The screeching sound when a modem connected was two modems negotiating which tones to use. You were sending data as sound.

CompuServe owned none of the wire. All the copper — the phone lines from your house to the local relay node, the leased lines between cities — belonged to AT&T and MCI. CompuServe rented it. The local relay nodes existed so you could make a local phone call instead of a long-distance one directly to Ohio. You called Chicago; Chicago bundled your call with others and forwarded it to Columbus on a dedicated leased line CompuServe paid for monthly.

Everything happened in Columbus. When you searched for weather, the Columbus mainframe looked it up and sent the text to your screen. When you sent an email, Columbus received it and stored it until the recipient logged in and retrieved it. When you played chess, Columbus ran the chess engine. Your computer displayed results. Columbus did everything else.

How the internet was added — one new wire

In 1989, CompuServe became the first commercial online service to connect to the internet — specifically for email. They ran one new leased line from the Columbus datacenter to an internet backbone connection point. Same type of wire they were already using. New destination.

Gateway software on the mainframe translated between CompuServe's internal mail format and standard internet email. When you sent a message to someone@university.edu, Columbus reformatted it and pushed it out through that new wire to the internet. When an internet email arrived addressed to your CompuServe user ID, Columbus caught it, reformatted it, and dropped it in your inbox exactly like an internal message.

This was the first crack in the wall. But CompuServe was still a walled garden — the internet gateway was a door, not a demolition. The rest of the service remained entirely private and controlled. It would take the World Wide Web, AOL's mass-market expansion, and eventually the collapse of the per-hour billing model to fully end the walled garden era.

Key terms
Walled Garden
A closed online ecosystem controlled by one company. Users can only access what the company decides to provide. CompuServe, AOL, and Prodigy were all walled gardens.
Modem
Modulator-demodulator. Converts digital data into audio tones for transmission over voice telephone lines, and converts incoming tones back to data.
Leased Line
A dedicated, always-on copper telephone connection rented from a phone company (AT&T, MCI) at a flat monthly rate. Unlike a normal phone call which charges per minute.
TCP/IP
The internet's core protocol. A shared language any computer can speak. What makes the internet "the internet" — an open standard owned by nobody.
Baud Rate
The speed of a modem connection, measured in signal changes per second. 300 baud ≈ 30 characters per second. 1200 baud ≈ 120. The difference between watching text trickle in versus appear.
Online Service
A commercial, subscription-based private network providing information and communication services via dial-up modem. The category CompuServe, AOL, and Prodigy all belonged to. Essentially extinct by 2000.

Era 01

The Walled Gardens

1985 — 1995
The Distribution Was the Product
Origin: AOL
AOL's software was slower and worse than alternatives. It won anyway because it put itself inside more mailboxes than any competitor could match. In markets where consumer attention is the scarce resource, distribution advantages compound faster than product advantages — and the mechanism for reaching the user is often worth more than what it delivers.
AOL CompuServe Netflix Facebook Google
+
The Story

By 1996, experienced internet users universally preferred the open web to AOL. The service was overcrowded, its content was limited, its dial-up access was slower than dedicated ISPs, and its interface was designed for the lowest common denominator. CompuServe's network was more reliable. Any regional ISP offered a faster, cheaper connection. In technical circles, AOL was a punchline.

AOL had 26 million subscribers anyway. The software was not the point.

At peak, AOL was manufacturing approximately 50% of all CDs pressed globally. Not as a music company — as a direct mail machine. Free trial discs arrived in cereal boxes, inside magazines, taped to PC magazine covers, inserted into hotel key card envelopes, bundled with frozen steaks from Omaha Steaks. The campaign cost approximately $300 million per year in disc production, fulfillment, and postage. In return, it delivered cold-start signups to people who would never have gone looking for an ISP themselves. The CD found them. They didn't find AOL.

This is what actually won the dial-up era. Not Keywords or Buddy Lists or "You've Got Mail." The CD campaign. It was a consumer goods problem solved with consumer goods logic: get onto every shelf, into every bag, through every door. The technology industry has rarely matched the distribution intensity of AOL's physical media strategy.

The lesson compounds in every direction. Netflix understood this when they built their DVD mailing infrastructure before building a streaming service — physical distribution built the subscriber habit, and streaming inherited it. Facebook understood this when they launched Platform, turning every third-party app into a Facebook acquisition channel. Google understood this when they paid Apple billions per year to be the default iOS search engine. The product doesn't reach the user without a mechanism to get there, and the mechanism is consistently undervalued relative to what it delivers.

The most common mistake is spending on product and assuming distribution will follow from quality. AOL's distribution was bad at delivering quality. It was extraordinary at delivering presence. And in consumer markets, presence precedes preference — not the other way around.

Pattern Occurrences
  1. 1993AOL begins aggressive CD distribution; grows from 200K to 1M subscribers within the campaign's first year
  2. 1995–98CD campaign peaks; AOL captures 66% of US internet traffic not through product superiority but through physical saturation of the mail channel
  3. 1997Netflix launches DVD-by-mail; the physical distribution model builds subscriber habits that the streaming product later inherits without needing to re-acquire trust
  4. 2000Peak: 50% of all CDs manufactured globally are AOL trial discs; estimated $300M/year in distribution spend — the largest physical software distribution campaign in history
  5. 2007Facebook launches Platform — turning developer apps into Facebook distribution channels; every app that integrates Facebook login is a funnel into Facebook's social graph
  6. 2010sGoogle pays Apple an estimated $10–15B/year to remain the default iOS search engine; paying for placement rather than earning it through competition alone
  7. 2020sApp store default placement battles (Spotify vs. Apple, Epic vs. Google) are fought as product disputes but are fundamentally distribution disputes — who controls access to the consumer
Era 02

The Portal Wars

1995 — 2000
The Index Beat the Garden
Origin: Yahoo
AOL built a walled garden of owned content and tried to keep people inside it. Yahoo built a directory and sent people out to the rest of the web. The internet's value compounded faster outside the wall than inside.
AOL Yahoo CompuServe Prodigy Netscape Time Warner
+
The Story

By 1995, two companies were on a collision course for the same prize — becoming the front door to the internet for ordinary people. They had identical user-facing goals (get people online, keep them there, sell them ads) but completely opposite strategies for how to get there.

AOL wanted to BE the internet. Yahoo just wanted to point at it.

AOL's bet was built around proprietary content. By the mid-1990s it had spent enormous sums building or licensing news, magazines, chat rooms, forums, games, email, and shopping — all branded AOL, all accessed inside AOL's own software, all unavailable to anyone who wasn't a subscriber. The famous Welcome screen with its grid of departments (News, Sports, Travel, Marketplace, People Connection) was the spiritual heir to cable television: a curated, premium, walled experience where every minute spent generated revenue. The model echoed CompuServe and Prodigy before it. The logic was sound: people want safe, organized, quality content — make them never need to leave.

Yahoo's bet was the opposite. Two Stanford grad students — Jerry Yang and David Filo — had started "Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web" in 1994 as a hobby, a hand-curated directory of links to other people's sites. They didn't host the content. They didn't license it. They just pointed at it. By 1995 it had become Yahoo!, a free homepage that did exactly one thing: tell you where else to go.

The two models put their costs in opposite places. AOL had to pay for every piece of content on its service — writers, licensing deals, server infrastructure, ongoing maintenance. Every new department was an expense. Yahoo's marginal cost to add another website to its directory was a few minutes of an editor's time, then nothing forever. As the open web grew, AOL's content costs grew linearly while Yahoo's barely moved.

The deeper asymmetry was network effects. Every new website that launched on the open web made Yahoo's product more valuable — more to find, more to organize, more reasons to start your day at yahoo.com. AOL got nothing from the wider web's growth; if anything, the wider web was a competitor pulling subscribers away. Yahoo benefited from every site that ever existed. AOL benefited only from the sites it owned.

By 1996, Yahoo had passed AOL as the most-visited destination on the open web. AOL's subscriber count kept growing through 2002 — the walled garden still appealed to families, beginners, and the recipients of AOL's relentless CD mailings — but its share of total internet attention was already in decline. The flat-rate $19.95 unlimited plan that supposedly saved AOL was the death sentence in disguise: once people weren't paying by the hour, they had no reason to stay inside AOL's content. They opened their browser, typed yahoo.com, and AOL became a dial-up tunnel rather than a destination.

AOL spent the next decade trying to fix this. It bought Netscape in 1999 for $4.2B to gain a foothold on the open web. It bought Time Warner in 2000 for $165B to acquire enough content to fill the garden. Both deals were catastrophes. The walled garden model had already been outflanked by something simpler — a directory page that admitted, in its very design, that it was not where you would spend your time.

The lesson recurs constantly. Walled gardens always lose to open networks once the open alternative becomes comparable in quality, because the open network benefits from the unbounded growth of everyone outside the wall. The walled garden's original strength — control — becomes its weakness, because control means you can never grow faster than your own ability to build.

Pattern Occurrences
  1. 1985 AOL founded as a proprietary online service for Commodore 64 users — the walled-garden model begins
  2. Late 80s CompuServe and Prodigy establish the same closed model: own the content, charge for access
  3. Jan 1994 Jerry Yang and David Filo start "Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web" — a hobby directory of other people's websites
  4. 1995 AOL hits 3M subscribers; Yahoo formally launches as a free homepage that links out to the open web
  5. 1996 Yahoo passes AOL as the most-visited destination on the open web for the first time
  6. Dec 1996 AOL switches to flat-rate $19.95 unlimited — paradoxically accelerating user migration to the open web (the meter is no longer running on staying inside)
  7. Mar 1999 AOL buys Netscape for $4.2B trying to gain a foothold on the open web — a defensive acquisition admitting the walled garden alone is not enough
  8. Jan 2000 AOL buys Time Warner for $165B trying to fill the garden with enough premium content to make it competitive — universally cited as the worst deal in business history
  9. 2002 AOL subscribers peak at 30M and begin a decade-long decline as broadband and Google make the walled garden obsolete
  10. 2009 AOL spun off from Time Warner — the walled-garden experiment formally ended; AOL becomes a content/ad company on the open web
Restraint Beat Maximalism
Origin: Google
When everyone in your category is racing to add features, simplicity becomes a moat that's almost impossible for them to copy without dismantling everything they've built.
Google AltaVista Yahoo Excite Lycos Infoseek
+
The Story

By 1998, AltaVista had a problem most companies would kill for: it owned web search. Founded inside Digital Equipment Corporation in 1995, it had become the definitive answer to "where do I find things on the internet" — fast, comprehensive, usable from a clean page that did exactly one thing.

Then it tried to become more.

Following Yahoo's lead, AltaVista convinced itself that search was a commodity, and that the real money was in keeping users on the site once they arrived. By 1999 the homepage was a wall of news headlines, stock tickers, weather, shopping links, classified ads, and email login — with the search box demoted to one element among many. The portal model promised higher engagement, higher pageviews, higher ad revenue. Every other major search engine made the same bet: Excite, Lycos, HotBot, Infoseek. None of them resisted.

Google, founded the same year, refused. Not because the founders had unusual discipline — they had no choice. Page and Brin were two grad students with one product and no resources to build a portal. The famously empty Google homepage with a logo, a search box, and two buttons wasn't a design philosophy; it was a constraint they were forced to embrace.

Then the constraint became the product. Users overwhelmingly preferred the empty page. It loaded fast on dial-up. It was clear what it did. The search results were better. Within four years Google had absorbed nearly all of AltaVista's traffic. By 2003, even Yahoo had quietly switched its own search backend to Google. AltaVista was sold to Overture for $140M — a fraction of its $2.3B implied 1999 valuation. By 2013, Yahoo killed it entirely.

The lesson is harder than it looks. AltaVista's portal pivot was not stupid — Yahoo built an entire empire on the same model, briefly worth $125B. The portal model worked when search was a commodity service inside a destination. It stopped working the instant one competitor proved that search done well was the destination.

The pattern repeats throughout internet history. WhatsApp beat Facebook Messenger by refusing to add anything. Notion beat Evernote by stripping features. Craigslist beat every "Craigslist killer" by never updating. When the category leader is busy adding capabilities, simplicity becomes a moat that's almost impossible for them to copy without dismantling everything that made them successful.

Pattern Occurrences
  1. 1996 Yahoo adds news, weather, sports, and email to its directory homepage, pioneering the "portal" template that defines the era
  2. 1998 AltaVista relaunches as a portal — stocks, news, shopping, classifieds — demoting the search box to one element among many
  3. 1998 Google.com launches with a deliberately empty homepage: logo, search box, two buttons
  4. 1999 Excite, Lycos, Infoseek all follow AltaVista into the portal model within months of each other
  5. 2000 Google's search market share crosses 30% on the strength of its minimalism alone
  6. 2003 Yahoo quietly switches its own search backend to Google — a tacit admission of defeat
  7. 2003 AltaVista sold to Overture for $140M, a fraction of its $2.3B implied 1999 valuation
  8. 2009 WhatsApp launches with intentional feature minimalism, eventually outscaling Facebook Messenger to 2B+ users
  9. 2013 Yahoo officially shuts down AltaVista, ending the portal-era pioneer entirely
Era 03

The Bubble Reset

2000 — 2003
The Biggest Deal Is the Most Desperate One
Origin: AOL
When a company at peak valuation executes its largest acquisition, it usually isn't expanding from strength — it's trying to buy what it cannot build, because it can see that its core model is about to become obsolete. The size of the deal is often proportional to the size of the underlying fear. AOL's $165B Time Warner acquisition is the canonical proof.
AOL Time Warner Microsoft Nokia Yahoo Verizon
+
The Story

By 1999, AOL's leadership could read the same industry reports as everyone else. Broadband was coming. DSL and cable internet were already 10–50× faster than dial-up. When broadband arrived in homes at scale, AOL's entire value proposition — the friendly, curated on-ramp to the internet — would become irrelevant. AOL was not a technology company in any meaningful sense. It was a distribution company with a consumer brand. Its model depended on being necessary at the on-ramp. Broadband would remove the on-ramp entirely.

The Time Warner merger was not a vision. It was a diagnosis and a response to that diagnosis.

The diagnosis: AOL's core business will be disrupted by infrastructure it cannot control. The response: acquire enough offline content value — films, cable infrastructure, news, music — that even when the internet access business dies, you survive. Time Warner had HBO. Time Warner had CNN. Time Warner had Warner Bros. and physical cable pipes. AOL's stock, at $164 billion, was the currency. The deal was announced in January 2000 — the absolute peak of AOL's valuation.

This is the tell. Companies use their own stock as acquisition currency when they believe their stock is overvalued relative to what they're buying. Paying $165 billion in stock for assets that the market would later value at $20 billion is not strategic genius — it is an efficient conversion of overvalued paper into real assets before the paper corrects. AOL's leadership understood the stock was not worth $164 billion. The Time Warner deal was, in part, a controlled exit from an unsustainable valuation.

The problem was that the merger didn't solve the actual problem. Broadband arrived. The content business (Time Warner's real assets) didn't need an internet company to operate it — and resented every aspect of the combination. The cultures were incompatible, the systems were incompatible, and the strategic logic depended on a "convergence" between internet access and media content that never materialized. AOL Time Warner recorded a $99 billion write-down in 2002 — the largest corporate loss in American history at the time.

What the merger demonstrates: a transformative acquisition at peak valuation, especially one that crosses industry lines, is a company announcing what it believes it cannot build organically. If AOL had believed its user relationships and technology could survive broadband, it would have invested in broadband technology. Instead, it traded all its chips for Time Warner's physical assets at the highest possible price. The market read this correctly — not as confidence, but as fear executing a very large transaction.

Pattern Occurrences
  1. Jan 2000AOL–Time Warner merger announced; $165B deal using AOL stock at its all-time peak — the largest merger in corporate history at the time
  2. 2001Merger closes as dot-com crash begins; AOL stock falls 90%; Time Warner shareholders lose estimated $100B+ in value absorbed via the stock-based deal
  3. 2002AOL Time Warner records $99B write-down — largest corporate loss in US history at the time; Jerry Levin resigns; Steve Case steps down
  4. 2009Time Warner spins off AOL; the merged entity lasted 9 years and destroyed more shareholder value than almost any deal in history
  5. 2013Microsoft acquires Nokia for $7.2B, desperate for mobile presence after missing the smartphone era; writes off $7.6B the following year — paying more than the company was worth to buy relevance it never achieved
  6. 2016Verizon acquires Yahoo for $4.5B; merges with AOL into "Oath"; writes off nearly the entire investment by 2018 — executing the same "buy what we lack" strategy on a smaller scale with similar results
Same Company, Two Completely Different Jobs
Origin: AOL
Employee stock options create two classes of worker — those whose hire date coincided with a low share price, and those whose hire date coincided with a high one. Skill and contribution are largely irrelevant to which class you're in. The most consequential variable in an employee's financial outcome at a high-growth company is something they had no control over: when the calendar said they started.
AOL AOL Time Warner Facebook Google
+
The Story

In 1993, if you got a job at America Online, your options were probably struck in the single digits — two, three, five dollars a share. By 1999, when AOL's stock hit $95, those options were worth life-changing sums. Engineers, product managers, and support staff who had joined during the early years — when the company was scrappy and the salary was below market — became millionaires. The lottery paid out for them.

In 2000, if you got a job at AOL, your options were struck at $75, $85, $92 per share. The dot-com crash had begun before many of those employees completed their first-year vesting cliff. The stock fell to $15. Every option was worthless — not depressed, not recovering, genuinely worth zero. These employees worked some of the hardest years in the company's history: navigating the Time Warner integration chaos, mass layoffs, and the collapse of everything that had made AOL a destination. They received nothing from their equity.

They were not less capable than the 1993 cohort. They were less lucky about the year on the calendar when they started.

This is not unique to AOL. It is the structure of every venture-backed or publicly-traded company where options vest over time. The financial outcome of working at a company for four years is almost entirely determined by when in the company's valuation cycle those four years occur. The 2010 Google employee whose options vested between 2010 and 2014 made far more than an equally-skilled 2021 Google employee. This is a structural feature, not a bug. The structure serves founders and early investors — the option pool is, in part, a mechanism for distributing risk to employees at the moment it is highest, in exchange for a claim on upside that may or may not materialize.

What makes this worth examining is the gap between how equity compensation is presented and what it actually is. It is presented as sharing in the company's success. What it actually is — in most cases — is a lottery ticket whose value is determined primarily by timing. Employees in 1993 didn't build a better company than employees in 2000. They arrived before the number went up. The underappreciated career skill of the technology industry is reading where a company is in its valuation cycle — not its product roadmap, its culture, or its opportunity, but its position on the curve between "worth nothing" and "worth everything."

Pattern Occurrences
  1. 1993America Online employees receive options at ~$2–5/share; those who exercise in 1998–99 convert into generational wealth
  2. 1999AOL stock hits $95; late-stage employees receive options struck at $60–95; the countdown to zero begins with no mechanism to unwind it
  3. 2001–02Stock falls to $10–15; all post-1998 AOL options expire worthless; affected employees had comparable performance to the cohort that retired early
  4. 2004–12Facebook employees across different join years receive wildly different outcomes; a 2004 employee's options are worth 500–1000× more than a 2011 employee's at the same vesting milestone
  5. 2020–21ZIRP era peak: hundreds of thousands of tech employees join at inflated valuations; options granted at $50B+ valuations fall underwater as rates rise 2022–23
  6. 2022–23Tech correction: Meta, Google, Amazon, Salesforce employees who joined in 2020–21 see options granted at cycle peak fall 40–70%; those who joined in 2018–19 are significantly above water on identical roles
Era 04

Search & Social

2003 — 2010
Every New Platform Is a Greenfield
Origin: AOL/AIM
AIM had 53 million users and was the default communication layer for an entire generation. It did not lose to a better AIM. It lost because the platform shifted from desktop to mobile, and the critical 2007–2010 window for forming messaging habits on the new platform closed before AIM shipped a competitive native product. Market dominance is real — but it does not transfer across platform transitions. Every new platform is a greenfield.
AIM AOL Apple WhatsApp Nokia Microsoft
+
The Story

By 2006, AIM was messaging. Not a major player in messaging — messaging itself. It had no meaningful competition on the desktop. ICQ had ceded the US market. MSN Messenger existed but was irrelevant outside specific demographics. Google Talk had launched in 2005 and hadn't taken hold. For anyone who grew up online between 1997 and 2006, the away message was their first piece of social self-expression, and the buddy list was how they knew who was available. The social graph of an entire generation lived in AIM's servers.

53 million users. Total category dominance.

Then the iPhone launched in June 2007.

Between 2007 and 2010, something happened that AIM could not control and did not respond to fast enough: mobile became the primary place people communicated. Text messages (SMS) were already eating into AIM's casual conversation volume. But the real threat was the new platform's open surface. On mobile, AIM was not the default. There was no default. Whoever shipped the best mobile messaging product in 2007–2010 would start building the new social graph.

AIM did ship on mobile. AIM for iPhone arrived. It was technically functional. But it was ported, not native — it assumed the conceptual model of a desktop application (a buddy list you logged into) rather than the mobile model (contacts drawn from your address book, always-on notifications, conversations that persisted whether or not you were "signed in"). Meanwhile, WhatsApp (2009) and the groundwork for iMessage (2011) were being built from mobile's assumptions up. They didn't need to unlearn the desktop paradigm because they had never been built for the desktop.

The crucial window was 2007–2010. This is when mobile social-graph formation occurred for the next cohort of users. Someone coming of age with a smartphone in 2009 formed their messaging habits on SMS and on apps that were native to the phone. AIM was the thing their slightly older siblings used on a laptop. By the time those users were old enough to choose a messaging platform, the choice had already been made by the products that had been waiting for them on mobile.

AIM shut down on December 15, 2017. Not because a superior AIM-like product beat it. Because mobile was a new platform, habit formation on the new platform occurred during a specific window, and AIM's product did not win that window. Its 53 million desktop users were a substantial asset on the old platform and were nearly useless on the new one.

The pattern repeats across every major platform transition. Internet Explorer's 95% browser dominance did not transfer to mobile. Yahoo's search dominance did not transfer to the social era. Nokia's 40% global phone market share did not transfer to smartphones. BlackBerry's enterprise messaging dominance did not transfer to iOS. In each case, the incumbent had the resources, the user relationships, and the brand. In each case, the window for forming habits on the new platform closed while they were still trying to port their existing product forward.

Pattern Occurrences
  1. 1997AIM launches as a standalone free download; desktop messaging begins its decade of dominance
  2. 2003AIM reaches 53M users; no viable competition on the desktop; the social graph of a generation is encoded in its buddy lists
  3. Jun 2007iPhone launches; mobile becomes the new platform; the habit-formation window for mobile messaging opens
  4. 2009WhatsApp launches, built natively for mobile; no buddy list, no "signing in" — contacts come from your phone's address book
  5. 2007–10Critical window: AIM for iPhone ships but feels ported; the next cohort of users forms messaging habits on SMS and mobile-native apps instead
  6. 2011iMessage launches as the default iOS messaging layer; by making mobile messaging frictionless for hundreds of millions of users, Apple closes the window definitively
  7. Dec 2017AIM shuts down; 20 years of operation ends with a blog post; the 53M user social graph it once held has long since migrated to platforms that were native to the new paradigm
  8. ParallelNokia at 40% global phone market share in 2007; 0% smartphone relevance by 2013 — dominant on the old platform, absent on the new one
  9. ParallelInternet Explorer at ~95% browser share in 2004; irrelevant on mobile; Chrome builds dominance from scratch on the new platform

AOL

1985 — present · The Walled Garden
FOUNDED 1985 · PEAK 30M SUBSCRIBERS · MARKET CAP $224B AT 2000 PEAK

For a decade, AOL was the internet for most American families. Then broadband killed dial-up, Google killed the walled garden, and the Time Warner merger killed the company.

Founded 1985 in Vienna, Virginia by Steve Case — originally a Commodore 64 service called Quantum Computer Services. Built around proprietary content (news, chat, email, sports, shopping) wrapped in a famously friendly Windows 3.1 interface that anyone could navigate. The free-trial CDs, the dial-up handshake, the Welcome Screen department grid, and the "You've Got Mail!" jingle became the visual and sonic vocabulary of an entire generation getting online for the first time.

Legacy & Firsts
  • Made the internet a consumer productBefore AOL, getting online required technical knowledge and a tolerance for command lines. AOL gave 27 million people a friendly front door — and the instinct that the internet should just work.
  • Invented the modern chat layerAIM and ICQ weren't features. They were the template. Presence indicators, away messages, the buddy list, the screen name as identity — every messaging app since has inherited this grammar.
  • Pioneered the free-trial-by-mail model50% of all CDs manufactured globally in the mid-1990s were AOL discs. Mailing physical media to tens of millions of households normalized frictionless software distribution and created a playbook cloud companies still adapt.
  • Proved the walled garden — and its ceilingAOL's proprietary content model is the ancestor of every closed platform since: Facebook's News Feed, the App Store, WeChat's super-app. AOL also demonstrated why they all eventually crack: the open internet is always bigger than any single garden.
  • Made email personalBefore AOL, email was for businesses and universities. "You've Got Mail" turned it into a human moment — the sound of someone thinking of you. The cultural weight of that small phrase outlasted the company by decades.
The Story · 1985 — 2026

From dial-up monopoly to private equity portfolio

Forty-one years in chronological order. From a Commodore 64 service called Q-Link, to 30M subscribers and 50% of all manufactured CDs, to the worst merger in history, to a Verizon checkbook, to Apollo Global Management. Every chapter that built AOL up and the ones that took it down.

Service Brand

Quantum Link rebrands. The name that becomes synonymous with going online for a decade.

Period

The story
The rebrand from QuantumLink came with a Windows client, a phone number, and a mission to put the internet in front of ordinary American families. The name change was a statement of intent: the internet would be for everyone, not just hobbyists and engineers.
Legacy
At its 2002 peak, 26.7 million Americans subscribed. "Are you on AOL?" meant "are you online?" for an entire generation. The brand has outlived the company, two corporate owners, and the dial-up era.

The story
Voice actor Elwood Edwards recorded "Welcome," "You've got mail," "File's done," and "Goodbye" in his Cincinnati living room at his wife's suggestion. She worked at AOL. He was paid $200. The warm voice turned email from a utility into a social moment.
Legacy
Probably the most recognized computer sound in history. The 1998 Nora Ephron film named after it confirmed the phrase had escaped into permanent vocabulary. "You've got mail" carries the full emotional weight of the early internet era in three words.

The story
AOL Keywords were proprietary shortcut addresses for content areas within the service — type "News" in the keyword bar and you arrived instantly, no URL required. It was navigating by intent before that phrase existed. Thousands of keywords existed; companies paid for premium placements.

The story
A persistent real-time view of which friends were online and what their away message said. Before it, you'd send an email into a void. After it, you could see who was there. Knowing someone was "Away: studying (not)" was a genuinely new kind of social signal.

Messaging

Instant Messenger. Defined teen internet for a decade. Killed Dec 2017.

The story
AIM began as a standalone download — free for anyone, not just AOL subscribers. Screen names became digital identities. Away messages were proto-social media. The running man logo was ubiquitous. At its 2006 peak: 53 million users. For an entire generation, it was the first place they had an online identity.
Legacy
AIM invented the social grammar every messaging app since has inherited — presence, away messages, screen names as persistent identity, group chats. Facebook Messenger, iMessage, WhatsApp, Discord: all trace back in a direct line. Shut down December 15, 2017 with a brief blog post.

AOL Hometown

Discontinued
·
Personal Pages

AOL's GeoCities answer. Millions of personal homepages. Killed 2008 — pages deleted with weeks notice.

tap to open →
Period
1996 – October 31, 2008
The story
AOL's personal homepage hosting platform — a walled-garden precursor to Myspace. Users built pages using AOL's tools on AOL's servers, with no presence on the open web. Millions of personal pages, photo albums, hobby sites, and family histories lived exclusively inside Hometown.
What ended it
Shut down October 31, 2008 with weeks of notice, deleting all user content permanently. Millions of pages vanished overnight. One of the earliest and most dramatic demonstrations of platform dependency risk — when a company that hosts your content shuts down, your content dies with it.

The story
AOL Search was never a genuine search engine — always a distribution layer surfacing results from partners. First Excite, then Google, eventually Ask.com. AOL had the traffic to make search matter but never built the technology to own it. The 2002 Google deal — AOL paid $1 billion to license Google's results — funded Google's infrastructure expansion.
What ended it
By 2009, search was entirely Google's. AOL had no technology of its own. The deal that was meant to improve AOL Search had instead made Google indispensable to AOL's users — and then to everyone else's.

The story
A set-top box that brought AOL's interface to the television: email, AIM, and browsing from the couch. Launched precisely as the Time Warner merger closed, which was supposed to deliver cable distribution and content to make the convergence vision real. Neither materialized.
Why it failed
The Time Warner integration never worked. Navigating the internet with a TV remote was deeply painful. Broadband was already making the model obsolete. The box sold poorly. Pulled in 2002. Period

The story
Google Reader shut down July 2013. AOL Reader launched June 2013 to fill the void. It was functional and fast — but Feedly, Digg Reader, and others had already captured displaced Google Reader users in the preceding months. Arriving second into a crisis-driven market requires exceptional speed.
What ended it
Shut down September 2015. RSS was a shrinking market, the audience was small, and Verizon (which by then owned AOL) had no strategic reason to maintain it. A reminder that "filling the gap left by a giant" is harder than it sounds — the gap fills faster than you can ship.

Revenue · Net Income · Market Cap · Enterprise Value

$ billions · fiscal years · Chart capped at $8B — market cap peaked at $164 billion in Jan 2000 before losing 97% of that value within two years. 2001–2009: subsumed into Time Warner, not independently reported.

Follow the Money

Every dollar, traced

A visual trace of where money actually went across AOL's entire story. The gold curve is paper market cap — what investors believed the company was worth at each moment. The blue band is real subscriber cash. The destinations below show where each type of money ultimately landed, and who was holding when reality arrived.

Note on scale: The gold bubble uses a square-root scale so the $164B peak doesn't compress everything else into invisibility — each unit of vertical height represents an increasing dollar amount. Real cash flows (blue/green/red boxes) are shown at approximate relative sizes. The key distinction: paper value that was never converted to cash is not the same as real cash that changed hands. Most of what was "lost" in AOL's crash was paper — but investors who bought at peak with real dollars lost those dollars permanently and irrecoverably.

Winners and Losers

The economic anatomy of AOL

Market cap is not money — it's a number that exists only as long as someone is willing to pay it. When $200 billion in AOL Time Warner value evaporated between 2000 and 2002, that wealth didn't simply vanish: some of it had already been converted into real cash by insiders who sold early. The rest was absorbed by whoever was holding the stock when reality arrived. CEO salaries, severance packages, and consulting contracts are paid in full regardless of outcome — meaning the people most responsible for strategy often bear the least financial consequence. What follows tracks where the actual dollars landed.

Major Win

AOL Founders & Pre-IPO Employees

Estimated extraction: $2 – 6B+

Steve Case, Jim Kimsey, and the founding team held options struck in the single digits. By 1999, AOL stock hit $95. Those who sold on the way up converted paper into permanent wealth. Case alone sold over $100M in shares in the period surrounding the merger announcement — a transaction that looked prescient in retrospect, since the stock he received Time Warner shareholders lost 90% of its value within two years. Early engineers and product managers who joined in 1992–1995 and exercised options before 2000 received life-changing sums.

Win (with conditions)

Early Venture Investors

Return multiple: 100x – 500x on early positions

America Online's early capital came largely from Mitsui and other strategic investors before a meaningful VC round. Those who got in at seed and Series A prices and sold anywhere in the 1997–2000 window made extraordinary returns. The condition: if they held through the merger and the crash, or if they received AOL stock in exchange for portfolio companies they sold to AOL, those gains largely reversed.

Operational Win

Third-Party Vendors & the CD Economy

Estimated annual transfer: ~$300M/yr at peak

At its peak, AOL was manufacturing roughly 50% of all CDs pressed globally — not because it was a music company, but because of its free-trial disc campaign. The money that flowed to disc manufacturers (3M, TDK, Ritek), fulfillment houses, and postal carriers was real and permanent. These vendors extracted hundreds of millions per year from subscriber revenue and investor capital. They bore zero risk when AOL declined. The CD was the most efficient transfer mechanism in the story.

Late Win

Post-Spinoff Shareholders (2009 – 2015)

Return on re-listing: +76% peak-to-Verizon

When AOL re-listed as an independent company in December 2009, shares opened around $25. Verizon acquired the company for $50/share in June 2015 — a clean 2× for anyone who bought on the re-listing and held. This cohort had no exposure to the original bubble and benefited from a leaner, restructured business. Apollo Global Management then bought Verizon's media assets (including AOL) for $5B in 2021, further rewarding late-cycle holders.

Catastrophic Loss

Time Warner Shareholders

Value destroyed: ~$100B+

The AOL–Time Warner merger is widely cited as the single worst major corporate deal in history. AOL, valued at $164B at its peak, acquired Time Warner using its own overvalued stock as currency. Time Warner shareholders received AOL shares that lost 90% of their value within 24 months. The business of Time Warner — cable, magazines, films — was real and profitable. It was acquired by a company whose primary asset was subscriber momentum that was already stalling. Jerry Levin, the Time Warner CEO who approved the deal, was later named worst CEO of all time by multiple business publications. He resigned in 2001.

Major Loss

Retail & Institutional Investors at Peak

Market cap destroyed: ~$200B (2000 → 2002)

Anyone who bought AOL or AOL Time Warner stock between mid-1999 and the merger close held a position that lost 70–95% of its value. This wasn't a sophisticated-investor-only problem: pension funds, 401(k) plans, and index funds held massive AOL Time Warner positions. The CalPERS pension, the Teachers' retirement system, and millions of ordinary American retirement accounts absorbed real, permanent losses. The money that insiders had already converted to cash had come, ultimately, from this pool.

Total Loss

Late-Cycle Employees (Hired 1999 – 2002)

Option strike prices: $60 – $95/share · stock went to ~$10

Employee stock options are only worth something if the strike price is below the market price. Employees who joined AOL or AOL Time Warner in the bubble years received options struck at $60–$95 per share. When the stock fell to $10, every one of those options was worthless — not merely reduced, but completely valueless. These employees worked during the hardest period of the company's history and received nothing from their equity compensation. Their salaries were paid, but the deferred compensation — the reason many had joined — evaporated entirely.

Dilution Loss

Companies Acquired with AOL Stock

Worst case — Netscape: $4.2B in AOL stock → ~$420M by 2002

AOL made most of its major acquisitions using its own stock as currency — a rational strategy when that stock is overvalued, since you're trading an overpriced asset for a real one. Netscape shareholders who accepted AOL stock in the $4.2B acquisition (Jan 1999) saw that stock lose 90% of its value. The same applied to shareholders in Moviefone, MapQuest, and others who received AOL shares. Those who negotiated cash terms or sold their AOL stock quickly fared far better than those who held.

Extracted Regardless

Senior Executive Compensation

C-suite total comp (2000–2003): ~$400M+ across leadership

Executive salaries, bonuses, and severance are contractual obligations paid before any returns reach shareholders. During the years AOL Time Warner destroyed $200B in market cap, its executives continued receiving eight-figure compensation packages. Bob Pittman received ~$50M in severance when he resigned in 2002. Jerry Levin's departure package was reported at approximately $800M in vested compensation accumulated over his Time Warner career. These were not outcomes tied to shareholder performance — they were structural extractions that occurred regardless of what happened to the stock.

Partial Recovery

Bondholders & Secured Creditors

Recovery rate vs. equity: significantly higher

Debt is senior to equity in any corporate capital structure. AOL Time Warner carried significant debt loads, but its underlying businesses (cable, magazines, films, internet subscribers) generated real operating cash flow. Bondholders — banks, insurance companies, institutional lenders — recovered substantially more than equity holders, and in many cases were made whole. The debt market was partially insulated from the equity collapse because the real operating business continued to generate revenue even as the stock became worthless.

CompuServe

1969 – 2009 · Columbus, Ohio · The Original Online Service

CompuServe was the internet before the internet existed. Founded to monetize idle mainframe time overnight, it became the world's first major commercial online service — where subscribers paid by the minute to read wire news, trade stocks, file-transfer software, and argue in forums organized by subject. It invented the GIF format, built the first consumer chat rooms, and established the architecture for every online community that followed. At its peak, 3 million subscribers paid premium hourly rates for the privilege. Then AOL arrived with a free CD, a flat monthly price, and a Windows interface — and CompuServe's precision metered model became an artifact within five years.

Legacy & Firsts
  • Invented real-time online chatAlexander "Sandy" Trevor coded CB Simulator over a single weekend in 1980 as a skunkworks project — no formal product mandate, no committee, just curiosity about whether the network could handle bidirectional real-time text. It became CompuServe's most popular feature. Every modern messaging app inherits its channel architecture.
  • Invented GIFSteve Wilhite built the Graphics Interchange Format in 1987 because CompuServe needed one image format that worked on Apple IIs, IBM PCs, and Commodore 64s simultaneously. "We didn't want to have to put up images in 79 different formats." The LZW-compressed format debuted June 15, 1987. It is still actively used — more widely now than it was then.
  • Built the first commercial online community modelCompuServe's Special Interest Groups (SIGs) were the first large-scale forums organized by topic and moderated by contracted community operators (sysops). The model — topic-organized discussion, voluntary moderation, self-selecting membership — is Reddit's model, Discord's model, and every modern forum's model.
  • First consumer internet email gatewayIn 1989, CompuServe became the first major consumer service to bridge the gap between its private network and the wider internet, allowing subscribers to send and receive email to and from internet addresses. The numeric format (71234,5678) became a status symbol in technical communities.
  • First commercial electronic shoppingThe CompuServe Electronic Mall launched in 1984 with over 110 retail storefronts — nearly a decade before the World Wide Web existed. Customers browsed, ordered, and paid online. Amazon would not exist for another ten years.
The Story · 1969 — 2009

From idle mainframes to AOL's checkbook

Forty years end to end. A side business selling overnight compute on insurance-company mainframes becomes the first consumer online service, dominates for seventeen years, and gets absorbed by AOL for $1.2B in 1997. The network finally goes dark in 2009.

→ scroll →
Idle mainframes, profitable evenings
Harry Gard and son-in-law Jeffrey Wilkins found Compu-Serv Network in Columbus, Ohio — selling overnight access to Golden United Life Insurance's mainframes to businesses that need computing time but can't afford their own hardware.
1969
Name changes. Ambition doesn't.
The board renames the company CompuServe Incorporated. By now it's selling time-sharing services directly to businesses across the country. The consumer market doesn't exist yet. They'll build it.
1977
First consumer dial-up service
CompuServe launches a consumer service for Radio Shack TRS-80 owners. $5 per hour off-peak. To access it, you dial a local phone number, hear noise, and find yourself inside something that has no name yet.
1979
H&R Block pays $25 million
The tax-prep giant acquires CompuServe — fewer than 1,000 consumer subscribers at the time. Within four years, the subscriber base reaches 110,000. H&R Block's distribution network and financial backing prove decisive.
May 1980
CB Simulator: the weekend that changed everything
Sandy Trevor codes a multi-user real-time chat system over a single weekend. He names it after CB radio. There are channels. There are handles. Strangers type at each other and call it a community. The template for every chat application ever built.
Jul 1980
Forums launch. The sysop economy begins.
Special Interest Groups go live — topic-organized forums moderated by contracted sysops who earn a share of forum revenue. CompuServe doesn't hire the moderators; it licenses the infrastructure to them. The model scales without headcount.
1981
Online newspapers and real-time wires
The New York Times, Washington Post, San Francisco Chronicle — all available on CompuServe before most people own a personal computer. Reading one costs $5/hr. The full text of a 20-cent newspaper takes two hours to download. Nobody cares. It's the future.
1983
Electronic Mall: 110 storefronts, no building
The world's first commercial online shopping mall opens. More than 110 retailers. Customers browse, order, and pay — nine years before Amazon exists, fifteen years before most people know what an online store is.
1984
GIF
Steve Wilhite's Graphics Interchange Format debuts. LZW compression. 256 colors. Works on every platform. "We didn't want to put up images in 79 different formats." GIF becomes universal before the web exists. It is still universal today.
Jun 1987
Largest online service on earth
380,000 subscribers — more than twice its nearest competitor. The Dow Jones News/Retrieval has 320,000. GEnie has 70,000. By any measure, CompuServe is the internet. The web doesn't exist yet. AOL has under 100,000 users.
1987
First internet email gateway
CompuServe becomes the first major consumer service to bridge its private network to the wider internet. The address format — 71234,5678 — becomes a mark of distinction among technical users. Half a million US subscribers. No other service is close.
1989
The last year as the clear leader
1.5 million subscribers. $290M+ in revenue. Full internet access — FTP, Usenet, then the Web. CompuServe is also technically superior to anything else available. AOL has 600,000 subscribers and is growing at 20% per month.
1993
AOL overtakes. The math changes.
AOL passes 3 million subscribers. CompuServe has the same. But AOL is adding a million users a year on a flat-rate model. CompuServe is adding hundreds of thousands on a per-hour model that punishes heavy usage. The professional audience isn't enough.
1995
Flat rate. Too late.
CompuServe introduces $9.95/month unlimited pricing to compete with AOL's $19.95 flat rate. The premium metered model that sustained CompuServe's business for 15 years is abandoned. It does not stem the subscriber decline.
1996
H&R Block sells. WorldCom buys. AOL buys.
In a two-step deal, H&R Block sells CompuServe to WorldCom for $1.2B. WorldCom immediately flips the consumer business to AOL for stock — AOL wanted the subscribers, WorldCom wanted the network infrastructure. CompuServe ceases to be independent.
Sep 1997
CompuServe Classic shuts down
After 40 years. After CB Simulator and GIF and the Electronic Mall and the SIGs and the numeric addresses and the metered hours. After 3 million subscribers paying $12.80 an hour. AOL posts a brief notice. The service closes.
Jul 2009
Infrastructure · 1985

How CompuServe actually worked

A privately owned network built on DEC PDP-10 mainframes in Columbus, Ohio. Local access nodes in 300+ cities connected by leased AT&T lines. Every subscriber routed through Columbus. One point of failure. Zero downtime in commercial operation.

300+Local access cities
PDP-10Core mainframe
56 KbpsLines leased from AT&T
1989Internet gateway added
The PDP-10
CompuServe built its entire service on DEC PDP-10 KL-10 processors — hardware designed for time-sharing that could serve hundreds of simultaneous users from a single machine. The choice of PDP-10 defined CompuServe's architecture, its costs, and ultimately its decline. Software House's System 1022 database ran on this hardware exclusively.
The local node network
CompuServe's price structure depended on local phone calls being cheap. They built a network of local access nodes — CompuServe-owned relay hardware in 300+ cities — so subscribers paid local phone rates to connect. The alternative was a long-distance call to Columbus. The node network was the invisible infrastructure that made CompuServe's pricing work.
All roads led to Columbus
Unlike later distributed internet architecture, everything on CompuServe ran on hardware in Columbus, Ohio. Every forum post, every email, every stock quote, every GemStone combat action — all processed in one building. The system had no geographic redundancy. It also had 99.97% uptime. The engineers were very good at what they did.
The 1989 internet gateway
CompuServe was the first consumer service to offer internet email — connecting subscribers to addresses outside the private network in 1989. The subscriber address format (71234,5678 — note the comma, not the period) became a status symbol in technical communities. The comma was a CIS peculiarity that distinguished it from every internet address that followed.
Acquisitions

Who they bought — and who bought them

CompuServe made seven acquisitions over its life — most were small technical companies absorbed to build capability. Three ownership changes defined its fate. Companies CompuServe acquired sit below the line; companies that acquired CompuServe sit above.

Products

What they built that lasted

Most of CompuServe's products are dead. The formats they created are not.

1980

CB Simulator

★ Iconic
·
Social Layer

Sandy Trevor coded it over a weekend in 1980 as a skunkworks experiment. Real-time multi-user text channels. Named after CB radio. Became CompuServe's most popular feature immediately.

tap to open →
Period
1980 – 2009 · 29 years
The story
Trevor didn't have approval. He just wanted to see if the CompuServe network could handle simultaneous bidirectional text from multiple users. It could. He named the channels after CB radio frequencies. Subscribers immediately formed communities, relationships, and support networks through typed conversation — before any of those concepts had names on the internet. CompuServe's engineering culture of "skunkworks projects" produced its most enduring product from an unsanctioned weekend experiment.
Legacy
Every modern messaging application inherits CB Simulator's channel architecture: topic-organized channels, handles instead of real names, real-time bidirectional presence. AIM, IRC, Slack, Discord — direct descendants. Sandy Trevor also initiated the request that produced GIF seven years later.
1980
Jun 1987

GIF

★ Universal · Still alive
·
Technical Standard

Steve Wilhite's Graphics Interchange Format. Debuted June 15, 1987. LZW compression. 256 colors. One format for every platform. Still the default for looping animation across the entire internet.

tap to open →
Period
June 15, 1987 – present · 37+ years and growing
The story
Sandy Trevor commissioned it: "We didn't want to have to put up images in 79 different formats." Apple, IBM, and Commodore each had proprietary image types — incompatible, bloated, useless on other hardware. Wilhite found LZW compression in a technical journal and built a format around it that was small, fast, and hardware-agnostic. He named it GIF (pronounced "jif," like the peanut butter — "Choosy developers choose GIF"). It debuted in CompuServe's CIM software. When Mosaic added the <img> tag in 1993, GIF was already on every platform. The web inherited it by default.
Legacy
The only technology from CompuServe's era that is in wider use now than it was then. Animated GIF wasn't initially intended — it emerged from the format's multi-image capability. Netscape added infinite looping in its browser. Reddit, Twitter, and Tumblr gave it a second life. Wilhite received a Webby Lifetime Achievement Award in 2013. He died in March 2022, aged 74.
Jun 1987
1981

Forums (SIGs)

Foundation
·
Community

Special Interest Groups — topic-organized communities moderated by contracted sysops earning a share of forum revenue. The architecture Reddit, Discord, and every modern forum still uses.

tap to open →
Period
1981 – 2009 · 28 years
The story
CompuServe didn't hire forum moderators. It contracted with sysops — community operators who built and managed their own topic areas (computing, aviation, medicine, science fiction, ham radio) and received compensation based on forum activity. The incentive structure was ahead of its time: CompuServe provided infrastructure, community specialists provided domain expertise. Forums had message boards, file libraries, and real-time conference areas. The model scaled without headcount.
Legacy
The SIG model is the template. Topic-organized communities, volunteer/contracted moderation, user-generated content as the primary value — Reddit is CompuServe's SIG architecture ported to the web. Discord is CB Simulator merged with SIG community organization.
1981
1982

CompuServe Mail

First
·
Communication

First called EasyPlex. Numeric addresses: 71234,5678. First consumer email that reached the wider internet (1989). The address format became a status symbol in technical communities.

tap to open →
Period
1982 – 2009
The story
CompuServe assigned each subscriber a unique numeric ID — two sets of numbers separated by a comma (like 71234,5678). For external internet email, the comma became a period (71234.5678@compuserve.com). The format was technical and inelegant. Subscribers didn't care. Having a CompuServe address in the mid-1980s meant you were on the network. In 1989, when CompuServe added the internet gateway, those addresses became globally reachable — the first time most consumers could receive email from anyone on the internet.
Legacy
CompuServe Mail bridged the gap between walled-garden proprietary email and the open internet email standard. The pattern — private service connecting to global internet — is what every modern email provider still does.
1982
1984

Electronic Mall

First
·
Commerce

The world's first commercial online shopping mall. 110+ retailers. Browse. Order. Pay. Nine years before Amazon. Fifteen years before most people knew what an online store was.

tap to open →
Period
1984 – 1996
The story
More than 110 retailers agreed to list products and accept orders through CompuServe's system — Sears, JCPenney, American Express, Bloomingdale's, Comp-U-Card. Customers dialed in, navigated text menus, and placed orders that were processed electronically. The merchandise shipped physically. The transaction happened online. This was 1984 — when a 2400-baud modem was fast and color monitors were optional.
What ended it
The Electronic Mall was sunset in 1996 as the World Wide Web made proprietary shopping interfaces irrelevant. Every retailer built their own website. The Mall's competitive advantage — being the only place to shop online — evaporated when the internet became the place to shop online.
1984
1983

CompuServe B Protocol

Technical standard
·
Infrastructure

Reliable file transfer over noisy 1980s phone lines. The de facto standard before Zmodem. Built because existing protocols failed on 1200-baud lines that weren't designed for data.

tap to open →
Period
1983 – mid-1990s
The story
Transferring a file over a 1200-baud modem in 1983 meant sending it over a phone line designed for voice, through switching equipment that introduced noise, delays, and corrupted data. Existing protocols (XMODEM) handled errors poorly. CompuServe's engineers built a protocol with aggressive error detection and retransmission designed for exactly this environment. Steve Wilhite — who would later build GIF — contributed to the wire protocol work. CompuServe B became the standard for its CIM client software and influenced later protocols.
Legacy
Superseded by Zmodem and later by internet protocols. But CompuServe's work on reliable data transfer over unreliable connections was a precursor to the error-correction and compression techniques that made dial-up internet viable in the 1990s.

Client Software

Windows CompuServe Information Manager. A graphical Windows client that arrived just as AOL was perfecting its own. Better than the text interface. Not enough to close the gap.

tap to open →
Period
1993 – 1997
The story
CompuServe had operated primarily as a text-based service since 1969. WinCIM brought graphical navigation, icons, and mouse-driven menus to CompuServe — a major departure from the command-line interface that had defined the service. It was genuinely good software. The problem: AOL had been shipping a polished Windows client since 1993 and had perfected it through millions of CD mailings. WinCIM was playing catch-up in a market where the gap was widening.
What ended it
WinCIM was replaced by CompuServe 2000 after AOL's acquisition in 1997. The rebrand attempted to make CompuServe competitive with AOL's consumer interface. By then, the subscriber trajectory was already irreversible.
1993

Dominant from 1969 to 1994 with no meaningful competition. Then AOL overtook it in a single year. By 1997, the web portals and AOL had made CompuServe's premium model obsolete.

Company Value · 1982 – 1997

Revenue · Market Cap · The arc

$ millions · fiscal years · CompuServe was profitable and growing through 1995, then flatlined as its hourly billing model became untenable. Sold to WorldCom at peak revenue — but the trajectory was already clear.

Winners and Losers

The economic anatomy of CompuServe

CompuServe's financial story is unusual in tech: the acquirer won decisively, the employees mostly moved on without catastrophe, and the company was sold at the optimal moment. H&R Block bought a time-sharing service for $25 million and sold a content network for $1.2 billion — one of the best corporate acquisitions in pre-internet tech history. The split of that $1.2 billion tells the story of what CompuServe actually was: the physical network was the valuable asset, and the consumer brand was what declined. AOL conflated the two. WorldCom understood the difference.

Major Win

H&R Block

$25M invested · $1.2B returned · 17 years

H&R Block paid $25 million for CompuServe in May 1980 when it had fewer than 1,000 consumer subscribers. Seventeen years later, they sold for $1.2 billion — a roughly 4,700% return before accounting for the profitable dividends CompuServe generated during its peak years. This is one of the highest documented returns on a corporate acquisition in the pre-dot-com era. H&R Block provided capital, distribution, and patience at exactly the right time. Their exit, in September 1997, was impeccably timed: CompuServe's subscriber base was already declining and the flat-rate pricing transition was destroying the hourly billing model that had made the service profitable. H&R Block sold at the peak and didn't look back.

Operational Win

WorldCom (MCI WorldCom)

Paid $1.2B total · Kept the network · sold consumer to AOL

WorldCom understood what it was actually buying. CompuServe had spent decades building a nationwide packet-switched data network — physical infrastructure connecting hundreds of cities with leased lines, switching equipment, and points of presence. That network was worth significant money to a telecommunications company. WorldCom paid $1.2 billion for all of CompuServe, immediately sold the declining consumer business to AOL for AOL stock, and kept the CompuServe Network Services division. The consumer division's sale partially offset the acquisition cost; the network was the prize. WorldCom's own collapse in 2002 (one of the largest bankruptcies in US history) eventually absorbed these assets, but as of 1997 the deal was textbook strategic acquisition.

Talent Win

Columbus, Ohio Tech Community

CompuServe trained 1,300 employees · many founded Ohio tech companies

At its peak, CompuServe employed 1,300 people in central Ohio — engineers, network operators, content producers, and business developers who had built, maintained, and grown the world's first major online service. The skills they developed — network engineering, online community management, distributed systems, consumer product design — were among the most valuable in technology in the mid-1990s. Many moved to internet companies, founded startups, or joined AOL. CompuServe's president Jeff Wilkins left in 1985 to found Metatec Corporation. The Columbus tech cluster that now includes major data centers for Google, Amazon Web Services, and Meta traces its lineage in part to the technical workforce CompuServe trained.

Subscriber Acquisition

AOL

Received: ~2-3M subscribers + European base · paid AOL stock

AOL's acquisition of CompuServe's consumer division was primarily a subscriber land-grab. CompuServe's 2-3 million subscribers — many in professional and business segments — were exactly the demographics AOL wanted. The European presence (850,000 subscribers in 1998) gave AOL meaningful international scale. What AOL did less well with was the brand: CompuServe Classic was maintained as a lower-tier service but received minimal investment. Its subscriber base eroded steadily. AOL shut down CompuServe Classic in July 2009. If AOL had paid cash rather than its own stock, the acquisition would have been considerably more expensive — using overvalued stock as currency was rational at the time but created accounting complexity when the stock crashed in 2002.

Lost a home

CompuServe Classic Subscribers

Service closed July 2009 · 30-year user community ended

Many CompuServe subscribers had used the service for fifteen to twenty years — some from the early 1980s. The forums, relationships, and communities they'd built inside CompuServe's Special Interest Groups had no equivalent elsewhere. When AOL shut down CompuServe Classic in 2009, subscribers lost not just a service but an entire social and professional network accumulated over decades. The financial loss was modest — it's the community loss that was real. CompuServe had maintained forums, mailing lists, and file libraries that predated the World Wide Web; when the service closed, that archive effectively disappeared. No export tools, no transition path, no equivalent destination.

Founders missed the exit

Harry Gard & Jeffrey Wilkins

Built the company · didn't hold for the $1.2B exit

Harry Gard and Jeffrey Wilkins co-founded CompuServe in 1969 using $1 million from Golden United Life Insurance. H&R Block acquired the company in 1980 — before the consumer service launched at scale — for $25 million. The founding team received their payout at that point: meaningful money, but a fraction of what CompuServe would ultimately be worth. Wilkins left in 1985 to found Metatec Corporation. Neither founder was present for the $1.2 billion sale to WorldCom. This is a structural pattern in early tech: founders whose companies are acquired early receive liquidity but miss the subsequent value creation they made possible. The $25 million in 1980 was a fair price for an unproven consumer service. It was a remarkable bargain in hindsight.

Follow the Money

Every dollar, traced

CompuServe ran on a single revenue model — hourly billing — for seventeen years. Every dollar a subscriber paid passed through five cost layers before reaching H&R Block, the parent company. In September 1997, that steady flow ended in one of the most elegant three-way deals in pre-internet M&A history.

ACT I · The Steady Flow · 1985 — 1996
ACT II · The Carve-Up · September 1997

The deal in plain English: WorldCom paid H&R Block $1.2B in stock to acquire all of CompuServe. The next day, WorldCom kept the Network Services division (its actual goal) and traded the consumer Information Service plus $175M cash to AOL in exchange for AOL's ANS Communications network division. H&R Block sold the WorldCom stock immediately at the dot-com peak. Two buyers, one seller, three prizes — H&R Block walked away with cash, WorldCom assembled a carrier-grade B2B network, and AOL erased its biggest consumer competitor. The CompuServe brand was the only thing nobody wanted.

The two leaders began with a handshake before cameras at the Villa Fleur d'Eau, then retired for what aides described as a one-on-one conversation expected to last well over an hour. The chip runs at 16MHz and can address up to 4 gigabytes of memory — far more than any current software requires. Industry analysts say it will power a new generation of "32-bit PCs" that could challenge minicomputers and workstations. Prodigy

1984 – 2001 · White Plains, New York · The IBM-Sears Experiment

Prodigy had the right ideas fifteen years too early — and the wrong business model for all of them. IBM and Sears built the first consumer graphical online service with flat-rate unlimited pricing before anyone else, a full in-house newsroom, color point-and-click navigation, Sears shopping, airline reservations, online banking, and multiple user IDs for the whole family. It was the closest approximation to the modern internet that existed in 1988. Then it tried to fund all of this with advertising. Every screen had an ad strip at the bottom. The model assumed users would passively browse content and generate ad views. Instead, they gravitated to email and bulletin boards — features that consumed network resources without displaying ads. When Prodigy charged for email beyond 30 messages, subscribers left in mass for AOL. IBM and Sears ultimately lost more than $1.3 billion on a service they sold for $200 million in 1996.
